https://www.hindustantimes.com/lifestyle.text: Built in the Middle Ages to provide shelter from attacks, Transylvania's fortified churches risk crumbling despite efforts to preserve and breathe new life into them.In a stark reminder, the outer wall of a historic church in the village of Mosna in central Romania visited by Britain's King Charles III in 1998 collapsed one night in June.Since then, Mariana Rempler, the village's last woman from the German-speaking Saxon minority, lives in fear that the church which attracts 4,000 visitors a year could also lose one of its towers."I felt a great pain inside me. It was as if I had collapsed at the same time with that wall," the 74-year-old told AFP, recalling the incident with tears in her eyes inside the church where she herself was baptised and wed.Mosna is one of the over 160 churches fortified with outer walls in Transylvania, built by the German minority so that the population in the then disputed border territory could take refuge from Tatars and Ottomans.As the Saxons left Romania, many to escape the communist dictatorship of Nicolae Ceausescu, several churches deteriorated with no one left to look after them.They are among historic monuments and other buildings in the eastern European country one of the continent's poorest to fall victim to neglect and decay.- 'New concept for survival' -Even edifices like Mosna, which underwent renovation after the fall of communism in 1989, remain in danger, with funds for more work difficult to find.Out of the 300,000 Saxons that lived in Transylvania before World War II, only about 10,000 remain today.About half of all fortified churches around 80, including Mosna have undergone restoration work in the last 35 years or will do over the next five years, Cristian Cismaru, manager at the Fortified Churches Foundation, told AFP.The foundation works with the Evangelical Church in Romania to preserve the historic monuments with grants and donations. Some 85 percent of the money comes from the European Union."I don't think we'll be able to address the other half of our heritage in our lifetime. That will be left for future generations," Cismaru told AFP at a brunch he organised with the local community for tourists, followed by a tour of the church in the village of Cincsor, 60 kilometres southeast of Mosna.He explained to participants that a third of the 30-euro entry ticket would be donated to a local development project."Our role, those of us who live in Transylvania, regardless of nationality, race or religion, is to continue to look after these monuments," he said."We want to breathe new life into these fortified churches."Cismaru added that many of the churches need "a new concept for their survival", since they can no longer function just as places of worship. One proposal is to turn them into cultural spaces.Earlier this month, fortified churches hosted dozens of events as part of the largest annual festival in Romania, dedicated to promoting the Saxon heritage, which drew a record of almost 10,000 visitors this year, according to organisers.- Photos of scattered bricks -In Mosna, mayor Dumitru Nutu says that after the wall collapsed even more tourists come to see the church, the village's main attraction."I keep seeing them from the town hall window. They're all taking photos of the broken wall," Nutu told AFP.Hundreds of scattered bricks, covered by a plastic sheet, are piled at the foot of the endangered tower, which was propped up with wooden beams in 2017."We reckon repairs will no doubt be carried out," said Francois Regis, a 53-year-old French tourist visiting with his wife, who described the church as beautiful and well preserved except for the northern part."The blend of Gothic and defensive elements is always interesting. All in all, the concept of a fortified church is quite intriguing."Like the tourists, Rempler also takes almost daily photographs of the tower, aiming to document the visible cracks and to urge speedy action."I'm afraid that in a month or two, that tower won't still be standing" with the wall no longer there to support it, she said.She hopes that the wall collapse will serve as a wake-up call and a solution will eventually be found."It would be a shame for us to let it fall into ruin."ani/jza/twThis article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

Photograph: Bianca De Marchi/AAP Sydney ‘Huge moment’: long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line to open next week The south-west metro extension will open on Friday 30 October, more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Wed 21 Oct 2026 16.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 16.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line will open next week, bringing an end to more than two years of replacement buses for residents in the city’s south-west. In a video shared on Instagram on Thursday morning, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced that the south-west metro extension would open on Friday 30 October. In a statement, the government said the first service would commence at 4.31am. Minns thanked “the thousands of commuters, families and local businesses for their patience while we’ve undertaken this major transformation.” “This is a huge moment for south-west Sydney,” he said. It comes more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line, which serviced 10 stations in Sydney’s inner west and south west – Marrickville, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Canterbury, Campsie, Belmore, Lakemba, Wiley Park, Punchbowl and Bankstown – closed in September 2024 to be converted to the driverless rapid transit system. ‘I’ve had enough of pink buses’: the long wait for Sydney’s newest metro line is nearly over Read more A continuous 66km metro line will span from Tallawong in the city’s north-west through the CBD to Bankstown in the south-west from next Friday. After regulator approval delayed the opening date of the city metro section in 2024, the Minns government had been at pains not to commit to a date for the south-west extension, despite media reports that it was aiming for launch on 18 October. Last week, the transport minister, John Graham, said that the opening was “very close” and “a matter of weeks, not months” after the operator, Sydney Metro, provided the final piece of safety data to the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR). The project to connect the stations to the city metro, which opened in August 2024, was estimated to take 12 months at that time. In the interim, commuters have had to use pink replacement buses to connect to metro services at Sydenham, where the line currently terminates. The government says the pink rail replacement buses will continue to operate on 30 October and the first weekend of operation. When the line opens, a journey from Bankstown to Central is expected to take 28 minutes – a six-minute saving compared with the former heavy rail line. Longer journeys are expected to yield greater savings, such as Lakemba to Victoria Cross, which will take 37 minutes – a 24-minute saving on previous travel times. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The government says the extension will deliver capacity for an additional 17,000 people during peak hours. Metro services run every four minutes during peak hours, five minutes during the day, and 10 minutes in the evenings and on weekends. The project has been delayed amid challenges in converting the 130-year-old heavy rail line and historic stations, including the need to add mechanical “gap-fillers” to fill spaces between curved platforms and trains. When the south-west metro opens, six of the 360 doors on the line where gaps are widest – three doors at Dulwich Hill, and one each at Marrickville, Canterbury and Campsie – will not be in use while data is collected on the reliability of the gap-fillers. The project was first announced by the former Coalition government in 2014. Labor campaigned against it at the 2019 election but committed to completing it after Minns became premier in 2023. Amid blowouts, the city and south-west metro sections are expected to cost more than $20bn combined. Photograph: Dave Thompson/PA Ofsted Headteachers consider leaving jobs earlier than planned after new Ofsted inspection Almost two-thirds of school leaders polled say new regime is much more intense than previous framework Sally Weale Education correspondent Mon 9 Nov 2026 19.01 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than half of headteachers in England who were polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are considering cutting short their careers as a result of the experience. In response to the question “Has the inspection affected how long you intend to stay in your role?”, 52% of those who responded said they were thinking of leaving their job sooner than planned. Amost two-thirds (64%) said the new inspections were “much more intense” than under the previous framework, while nearly nine in 10 (86%) struggled with their mental health and wellbeing while inspectors were on site. The findings from the survey by the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) are a damning indictment of the new regime that is the result of a radical overhaul after the suicide of the primary school headteacher Ruth Perry in January 2023. The changes, which were introduced a year ago, were intended to reduce the strain and workload caused by the inspection process, but many school leaders say they have made things worse. One primary headteacher who took part in the survey said: “Not sure my physical or mental health could cope with another inspection like this framework. Have been a head for 15 years across three schools and have never felt less able to do my job than I did during the inspection.” New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey says Read more A deputy head at an all-through school said: “I previously had aspirations for headship. I will now never go for headship. The stress and anxiety of the inspection has ended that dream … this is the most challenging Ofsted I have ever completed in a career of over 20 years.” A primary school chief executive said: “I’m very tired of the high stakes, the stress, the worry that comes from the whole process. It’s on a different level.” A headteacher at a secondary special school said: “I will not do another inspection as head. I will leave before the next one – it made too much of an impact on my personal life – I didn’t see my children for months on the run up to going into window.” The general secretary of the NAHT, Paul Whiteman, said the survey findings showed “the unmitigated failure of an unaccountable and out of control inspectorate” and said Ofsted’s actions were driving experienced leaders from schools. The education secretary, Lucy Powell, has indicated she is looking at further changes to Ofsted, but Whiteman said that “another belated rearranging of the deckchairs which sidelines the profession is wholly insufficient”. The survey, which had 242 responses between June and October, comes after teaching unions declared no confidence in the schools watchdog and threatened strike ballots unless significant wellbeing issues caused by the new inspection framework were fixed. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion An Ofsted spokesperson said many leaders had found inspections helpful and constructive over the last year, but acknowledged that others had highlighted the impact on their workload and wellbeing. “That’s why we’re working with the secretary of state on ways to reduce the pressure felt by heads and teachers, without losing our shared focus on the best interests of children and their families,” the spokesperson said. A Department for Education spokesperson said teachers do extraordinary work and inspections should support improvement without adding to pressures already on schools. “That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is collaborative, fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.” Explore more on these topics Ofsted Teaching England Department for Education Teachers' workload Schools news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints New Ofsted inspection regime is damaging our health, headteachers say Ofsted drops ‘clumsy’ and ‘offensive’ guidance linking autism and extremism Ofsted inspections pushing headteachers to ‘point of destruction’, union chief says Headteachers’ union considers strikes after judge rejects case against Ofsted Ofsted to press ahead with new inspection regime despite opposition Ofsted’s new inspection proposals are vague and out of date, say experts End to school rating system could play havoc with house prices, says Ofsted chief Headteachers in England threaten to quit as Ofsted inspectors over proposed overhaul Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students
